cards.back: The right action is the one that produces the greatest happiness for the greatest number.
Act utilitarianism judges each action by its consequences; rule utilitarianism follows rules that maximise utility if generally followed.
Measures pleasure by intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity, fecundity, purity and extent.
Intellectual pleasures are higher in quality than bodily pleasures: "better Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied".
Maximise the satisfaction of preferences rather than pleasure (Peter Singer).
Utilitarianism could justify harming a minority if it increases total happiness.
Moral rightness depends only on consequences.
A thought experiment against hedonism: we value more than pleasurable experiences.
Is it right to divert a trolley to kill one person instead of five? Tests consequentialism against deontology.
Morality is about duties and rules, not consequences.
Act only on a maxim you could will to become a universal law.
Treat humanity never merely as a means, but always also as an end.
Hypothetical: if you want X, do Y. Categorical: do Y whatever you want.
The only thing good without qualification: acting from duty.
Perfect duties must always be followed (don't lie); imperfect duties allow latitude (help others).

cards.front: Kant and the murderer at the door
cards.back: Kant held that lying is wrong even to save a friend.
Several duties (fidelity, non-maleficence, justice…) that can conflict: deontology without a single rule.
Kant's ideal community in which everyone treats each other as ends.
Focuses on character: what would a virtuous person do?
Flourishing, or living well; the final end of human life.
A virtue is the mean between two vices of excess and deficiency (courage between rashness and cowardice).
Practical wisdom: knowing how to act well in particular situations (Aristotle).
The human function is rational activity; living well is doing it with virtue.
It gives little action guidance in moral dilemmas.
Weakness of will: knowingly acting against one's better judgement.
There are objective moral facts independent of what anyone thinks.
Moral statements express feelings of approval or disapproval: "boo to murder".
Moral statements try to state objective facts, but all are false because there are no such facts.
Mackie: objective moral values would be metaphysically strange entities.
You cannot derive an "ought" from purely factual "is" statements.
For any natural property X, "Is X good?" stays an open question, so good is not X.
Moore: identifying goodness with a natural property.
Moral truths are relative to cultures or individuals.
Justified true belief.
Cases of justified true belief that are not knowledge, because the belief is true by luck.
Rationalists: some knowledge comes from reason alone. Empiricists: all knowledge comes from experience.
"I think, therefore I am": certain even under radical doubt.
A demon could deceive me about everything, so sense experience gives no certain knowledge.
The mind at birth is a blank slate; knowledge comes from experience.
There is no non-circular justification that the future will resemble the past.

cards.front: A priori vs a posteriori knowledge
cards.back: A priori knowledge is independent of experience; a posteriori knowledge depends on experience.
Knowledge rests on basic beliefs that need no further justification.
We perceive the external world directly, as it is.
Perception can be mistaken (a stick looks bent in water), so we do not directly perceive objects.
Mind and body are distinct substances (Descartes).
How do mental states relate to physical states of the brain?
Everything, including the mind, is physical.
Jackson: Mary knows all the physical facts about colour but learns something new when she sees red, so physicalism is incomplete.
A being physically identical to us but without conscious experience; an argument against physicalism.
Mental states are defined by their causal role, not by what they are made of.
Manipulating symbols by rules is not understanding; an argument against strong AI and functionalism.
The subjective, felt qualities of conscious experience (what red looks like).
How can a non-physical mind cause physical events? An objection to substance dualism.
Every event is causally determined, so free will does not exist.
Free will is compatible with determinism: acting on your own desires without external constraint.
Free will exists, and requires that determinism is false.
Examples meant to show that moral responsibility does not require the ability to do otherwise.
A person is morally responsible only if they could have done otherwise.
If determinism is true, our acts are consequences of the laws and the past, which are not up to us.
